portal.meta_desc: A parish-owned platform template. Locally hosted, no tracking, no advertising. Under the EVE Glyph Design doctrine.
portal.hero_h1: A parish website belongs to the parish.
portal.hero_lead: {count} parishes across four countries, one design canon, nine languages. Locally hosted. No tracking. No advertising. No third-party predators. Every dollar stays in the community.
portal.hero_p: Choose a parish to enter its site. Every parish site shares the same EVE Glyph Design canon, so navigation and typography stay familiar. Each parish's official site remains the source of truth — this is a mirror prepared with care, ready to be handed over to the parish's existing IT volunteer whenever they want it.
portal.ledger_lead: A running record of what people already do around here — a purchase, an hour of help, a favour from someone with a trade — so it adds up somewhere and the parish can see it.
portal.ledger_li1: Buy through the parish code, and the savings reach the parish.
portal.ledger_li2: An hour of help, signed off by one witness, is entered on the ledger.
portal.ledger_li3: Someone with a trade — plumber, accountant, nurse — can contribute their hour at its true rate.
portal.ledger_li4: One page, and the whole parish can read it.
portal.about_p: {count} Catholic parishes, each with a mirrored site under a shared editorial template. Same header, same footer, same navigation — but each parish keeps its own crest, Mass times, contact information and diocesan link. If a parish already has an IT volunteer, this is not a replacement; it is an option they can inspect, fork, or ignore.
portal.pillar1_p: Static site on GitHub Pages or the parish's own hosting. No third-party dashboard, no vendor lock-in.
portal.pillar2_p: No cookies. No analytics. No third-party scripts other than Google Fonts. Marked noindex, nofollow until the parish approves publication.
portal.pillar3_p: The parish owns its content, its own domain name and its own exit. Fork the repository, take it home, and carry on.
portal.pillar4_p: A shared EVE Glyph Design canon, so parishioners moving between parish sites feel at home.
portal.lang_p1: This surface is not English with translations attached. Every text is first carried to a single Latin baseline, and every other language is rendered from that baseline. Latin is the pivot because it is the language the Church already holds in common, and because a pivot means no living language is subject to another living language.
portal.lang_p2: Latin, English, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, Greek and Swahili. Greek is rendered from the Latin baseline just like every other language. Swahili is here because the platform is meant for all people, not only the wealthy — a person should be able to show this to their mother and sister in the language they actually think in, and be understood.
portal.lang_p3: Proper names, street addresses, telephone numbers and clock times are never translated. They are rendered exactly as the parish publishes them, in every language.
portal.kofc_lead: This is what scale within a week looks like — with no offense intended.
portal.kofc_p: If the Knights want to make parish web presence uniform across a diocese, this template can bring up a new parish site within about an hour. But that is not what is being offered. What is offered is a choice:
portal.kofc_li1_b: The existing IT volunteer stays in place.
portal.kofc_li1: If a Brother Knight or parishioner already runs the parish site, nothing is disturbed. This platform is available if they want to switch or fork it; otherwise it stands beside their existing work as a reference.
portal.kofc_li2_b: The money stays in the parish.
portal.kofc_li2: No annual hosting fees, no website subscriptions, no advertising credits. Static hosting is free, and every dollar the parish saves stays in the community.
portal.kofc_li3: No tracking, no engagement-optimized feeds, no algorithmic exposure of children, women or the vulnerable. A parish site is a parish site — not a data-extraction surface for a remote platform.
portal.kofc_li4: Ownership, doctrine and exit rights belong to the parish and its Council. The design canon is a shared reference, not a contract with a vendor.
portal.kofc_note: Council of Palms #6673 (Holy Trinity, Lenexa) is the reference council for this build.
portal.kofc_xref: The Charitable Ledger above is paired with the parish sites — that is the other half of what is offered.
portal.doc1_p: No parishioner is counted, categorized or targeted by this platform. Ever.
portal.doc2_p: The safety of content and identity comes before growth, engagement or profit.
portal.doc3_p: Design founder: {founder}, EVE Glyph Design. This credit is irrevocable.
portal.doc4_p: The parish binds the platform, receives a governance receipt, and may exit at any time with a full export of its content.

footnote.h2: A note — and who were the Acadians, anyway?
footnote.aside: Down here at the bottom, because it is a note, not a sales pitch.
footnote.p1: Long before all the parishes above, there was one at Port-Royal, in what is now Nova Scotia: Saint-Jean-Baptiste, founded 1613. Capuchin friars ran the mission from 1632. The first Catholic parish in what later became Canada.
footnote.p2: Then most of the records ceased to exist. In 1654 a force from New England, led by Robert Sedgwick, took Port-Royal, killed the Capuchin superior Léonard de Chartres and expelled his fellow friars — against the terms of the capitulation they had just signed. Two registers survive: 1702–1728 and 1727–1755, now at the Centre acadien of Université Sainte-Anne. Everything before 1702 has perished.
footnote.p3: The Greek card above is the other half of the same idea. In Nafplio, a wooden arch erected in 1841 carries the names of roughly 280 foreigners who died for someone else's homeland, each one with the place where he fell written beside it. Someone decided those names were worth keeping. In Port-Royal, someone decided ours were not.
footnote.p4: People ask whether Rome kept a copy. Rome handles governance, not the sacraments — there is no central baptismal register in the Vatican. Baptisms are recorded in the parish, full stop. When the parish burns, that is the end of it.
footnote.p5: One set, however, did make the journey. The registers of Saint-Charles-des-Mines from Grand-Pré went with the deported Acadians to Maryland, then to Louisiana, and were handed over to the priest at Fort San Gabriel in 1767. Today they sit in the vaults of the Diocese of Baton Rouge.
footnote.p6: And no, this is not a claim that we are the oldest Catholic anything in North America. St. Augustine, Florida has the year 1565 — it is the second card at the top of this page. San Miguel Chapel in Santa Fe is around 1610. Port-Royal is only the first one that is ours, and the one whose records were burned.

parish.saint-dunstan.status_note: Four churches have stood on this corner of Great George Street since 1816: the wooden chapel of 1816, a larger wooden cathedral from 1843, the stone cathedral dedicated in 1907, and the present basilica. A fire broke out in the sanctuary on the night of 7 March 1913 and consumed the roof and the whole interior; the walls and façade survived, and the church was rebuilt within its own stone shell and rededicated on 24 September 1919. Pius XI granted the title of basilica, conferred at the consecration of 26 June 1929 — a hundred years after the year the diocese was created. It has been a National Historic Site of Canada since 1990. Bishop of Charlottetown: Most Rev. Joseph Dabrowski, C.S.M.A. Knights of Columbus Our Lady of Fatima Council #824, founded in 1903 and the first council east of Montréal, meets here.

nafplio.location: The church stands in the Old Town of Nafplio, up the steps above the square of Agios Spyridon. The people of Nafplio call it the Frankoklisia — the church of the Franks. It belongs to {diocese}.
nafplio.history: The building was a mosque in the years before the Greek War of Independence was fought. In 1839 the Municipality of Nafplio ceded it to the Catholic Church by royal decree of King Otto, and in 1840 it was consecrated to the Transfiguration of the Lord — a name chosen to signify the transfiguration of the homeland itself after the Ottoman period. The mihrab still remains inside.
nafplio.arch_p: Inside the church stands a wooden arch, made in the shape of the front of an ancient temple, at the expense of the French philhellene Auguste Hilarion Touret. It carries the inscription A LA MEMOIRE DES PHILHELLENES MORTS POUR L'INDEPENDANCE and the names of roughly 280 foreign volunteers, each with the place where he fell written beside it. It is the oldest monument to the Philhellenes in Greece, and it was restored in 2002.
nafplio.crypt_p: Under the floor there is a Venetian cistern, about three metres deep. In 1839 the bones of philhellenes and of Bavarian soldiers, lost to typhoid fever in the years 1833–1834, were moved into it. In 1990 the relief Philhellenes Fighting for the Greeks, made by Nikolaos Dagoulis, was placed there.
nafplio.card_body: Faith lives where it stands, with a community that prays, celebrates and cares for one another.
parish.saint-dunstan-fredericton.tagline: The founding Catholic parish of Fredericton — first cathedral of New Brunswick
parish.saint-dunstan-fredericton.portal_: The founding parish of Catholic Fredericton, and the first cathedral of New Brunswick.
parish.saint-dunstan-fredericton.status_: St. Dunstan's is today the principal church of St. Mary Magdalene Parish, a united parish that also includes St. Columba at Fredericton Junction and Sts. John and Paul at New Maryland. Pastor: Rev. Peter Osborne; Bishop of Saint John: Most Rev. Christian Riesbeck, C.C. Parish mail is sent to PO Box 187, Fredericton, New Brunswick E3B 4Y9. A resident priest has served here ever since Fr. Michael McSweeney arrived in 1827, and the church built under Bishop William Dollard in the decade after 1840 was the first Roman Catholic cathedral in New Brunswick — Dollard was consecrated in it on 11 June 1843. When the Great Fire of 11 November 1850 consumed more than three hundred buildings in Fredericton, St. Dunstan's remained among the few churches left standing; parishioners are said to have held the roof against the embers with their own bodies. The present church, with its ninety-two foot tower, was consecrated on 15 August 1965. This parish sustained the French-speaking Catholics of Fredericton for sixteen years — French Mass twice a month from 1965, then a curate of St. Dunstan's assigned to them from 1978 — until Sainte-Anne-des-Pays-Bas was erected as a parish in its own right on 2 September 1981.

parish.paradise-village-mass-nuevo-valla: The English Sunday Mass by the marina at Nuevo Vallarta
The English-language Sunday Mass celebrated inside Paradise Plaza at Nuevo Vallarta, intended for the people of the marina area.
A standing Sunday Mass, not a canonically erected parish · Diócesis de Tepic · Decanato Bahía de Banderas
Diócesis de Tepic · Decanato Bahía de Banderas

This must be stated plainly: this is a standing Sunday Mass, not a parish. The Diócesis de Tepic, which holds jurisdiction over Bahía de Banderas, does not list it among its parishes or quasi-parishes, and no source names a priest or a parish that supplies the celebrant. It is a long-standing pastoral accommodation for English-speaking residents, condominium owners and visitors of the marina area, which meets inside the Paradise Plaza mall in the Paradise Village complex. The nearest canonical parishes are the Cuasiparroquia de la Sagrada Familia at Las Jarretaderas and Nuestra Señora Reina de la Paz at Bucerías. The Vallarta Yacht Club is about one kilometer to the north on the same Paseo de los Cocoteros; no source connects this yacht club with this Mass, nor does this card assert it. No founding date can be given, because nothing was ever founded — the listing in worship directories can be traced from around 2005 (the mid-first-decade of the twenty-first century) up to the present day. No freely licensed image of the Mass, of the Paradise Plaza interior, or of any chapel on site could be found. The only free image of the complex is a 2005 photograph of the gated entrance of that tourist site — a gate, not a church — and a gate on a church card would be a lie of composition. The card remains without an image until someone present on site sends one.

The Sunday Mass at 10:00 AM in English is confirmed by the PVAngels worship directory, by the Villa Encantada visitor pages, and by repeated first-hand witness reports, but no diocesan source publishes it. There is no parish office and no published telephone number. A separate interdenominational Christian service meets at 10:30 AM in the Salón del Sol of that tourist site — which is not this Mass.
parish.santa-cruz-huanacaxtle.status_not: Parish priest: Pbro. Luis Alberto Moreno Martínez, according to the clergy directory of the Diócesis de Tepic. Patronal feast: the third day of May, Día de la Santa Cruz. No primary source publishes a founding year for the parish; the gap is left open rather than invented. The postal code is C.P. 63732 according to the diocese, although several tourist directories publish 63734. No freely licensed photograph of the church exists: Wikimedia Commons, Wikidata, Flickr and KartaView street images within three hundred meters were reviewed, and none shows the face of the church. The card remains without a photograph until someone from the community sends one.
